alert.brief: A destructive alert 'Payment failed' with a description and a warning icon

votes.rationale: Second uses a tinted background to separate the alert from the page, has clearer text/icon color contrast, and adds actionable buttons (Update payment method, Dismiss) that make the alert's purpose and next steps obvious, while first is just an outlined box with no affordances.

Second has a tinted fill background separating the alert from the page, clear title/body/action hierarchy, and actionable buttons, while first is just an outlined box with plain text and no actions; second's design_slop fail is minor next to first's weaker overall composition and lack of affordances.

Second has a filled tinted background, actionable buttons, and clearer visual separation between title/body/actions, giving stronger hierarchy and clarity, while first is a flat white box with no actions; second's design_slop fail is minor next to first's icon_decorative fail affecting actual accessibility.

First adds actionable buttons (Update payment method/Dismiss) with clearer visual weight and grouping, while second is a plainer bordered box with no actions; both fail title_and_body but only second fails icon_decorative, and first's richer composition and affordances outweigh its design_slop flag.

First has a fuller, more resolved alert structure (tinted surface, bold title, body copy, and clear primary/secondary actions) versus second's bare bordered box with no actions; both fail title_and_body but second additionally fails the icon_decorative a11y gate.

First has clear title/body/action hierarchy with actionable buttons and better composition (filled background, spacing, grouped actions), while second is a bare bordered box with no action affordance and fails icon_decorative; first's title_and_body/design_slop gate failures are minor compared to second's weaker structure and failed accessible-icon gate.

FIRST renders a complete, well-organized app shell with a working sidebar, active nav state, and clear content hierarchy, while SECOND is a broken HTTP 500 error page that fails every gate check.

votes.rationale: Second uses bolder type and icon-labeled buttons for slightly stronger hierarchy and affordance clarity, but its design_slop gate failure (likely gratuitous color/icon styling) and less restrained composition tip overall craft to first.

Second has stronger color/icon accents and a clearer primary-action affordance, but it fails the design_slop gate and first achieves a cleaner, more restrained composition with equally clear labeling.

First uses bolder type contrast, an icon-color-to-button color echo, and icon-labeled buttons that read more clearly, but it fails the design_slop gate while second passes cleanly, giving second the edge on strict brief fulfillment.

First has a colorful icon tile and bold indigo CTA giving slightly stronger hierarchy/affordance, but it fails the design_slop gate while second passes all gates with a cleaner, more restrained composition and equally clear labeling.

filter_toolbar.brief: A filter toolbar: a search box with a leading icon and ⌘K hint, a sort dropdown, and a List/Grid view switch

votes.rationale: First groups the view-switch icons into one cohesive segmented pill and passes nearly every gate, while second's toggle reads as two mismatched boxes and fails composites/select/slop checks despite a nicer bolded sort value.

First groups the list/grid toggle into a single clear control with a visible active state and passes nearly every structural gate, while second's ungrouped view buttons, fake select, and stray caret artifact in the search box signal sloppier composition and worse accessibility (four gate failures vs one).

First is clean and its sort/view controls are real, grouped, gate-passing components, while second stacks a redundant sort icon plus fake dropdown (sort_is_a_real_select, composites_are_groups, design_slop all FAIL) that reads as visual clutter without added function.

Second passes real grouping and a genuine select/dropdown plus clean styling (only one gate fails, matching first), while first fails three gates including a fake sort control and ungrouped composite; first only edges out on clarity by visibly showing the current sort value ('Sort: Newest').

Second groups the list/grid toggle into a real segmented control and uses a genuine select for sort, matching the gate results (composites_are_groups, sort_is_a_real_select, design_slop all pass vs fail on first); first's decorative sort icon and ungrouped toggle read as slop.

Second passes real grouping/select semantics and shows a clear active state on the List/Grid switch, while first only differentiates via the bold sort value and fails three structural gates including a fake select.
